title: 04. Caching: TTL (Time To Live)
summary: TTL is a per-entry expiration timestamp attached to a cached value: after the TTL elapses, the entry is considered stale and is either returned conditionally (stale-while-revalidate) or evicted and re-fetched from the source —…
objectives: What is a TTL, and why is it the foundation of cache consistency?
What is the freshness-vs-load trade-off in choosing a TTL?
What is the thundering herd problem, and how does TTL jitter prevent it?
What is stale-while-revalidate (SWR), and how does it improve on plain TTL?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** TTL is a **per-entry expiration timestamp** attached to a cached value: after the TTL elapses, the entry is considered stale and is either returned conditionally (stale-while-revalidate) or evicted and re-fetched from the source — trading freshness for load and forcing the operator to pick a number on the freshness-vs-efficiency spectrum.

A TTL is the simplest possible consistency contract between a cache and its callers: "this value is good for N seconds, after which I won't vouch for it." Every entry written to the cache carries a deadline (write time + TTL), and on read the cache compares the deadline to the current time. If the deadline is in the future, the entry is fresh and served; if it has passed, the entry is expired and either evicted or served as stale while a background refresh happens. This is the only mechanism that lets a cache self-clean without explicit invalidation messages — every other policy (LRU, LFU, write-through) requires either capacity pressure or an external signal, but TTL guarantees an upper bound on staleness regardless of access patterns. That guarantee is what makes TTL the foundation of virtually every caching layer in production: DNS resolvers (A records with 86,400-second TTLs), browser HTTP caches (Cache-Control: max-age), Redis (EXPIRE / SETEX / PX), Memcached (the second positional argument to set), CDNs (Cache-Control headers honored at edge POPs), and even HTTP session cookies. Real-world: the DNS root servers publish A records with a 518,400-second (6-day) TTL; the .com TLD servers use 1,728,000 seconds (20 days) for delegation NS records; Cloudflare's edge cache uses TTLs from 30 seconds for breaking-news pages to 1 year for hashed static assets.

Choosing the TTL value is the core trade-off in cache design, and it maps directly to the staleness-vs-load dial. A short TTL (1–10 seconds) means cached data is nearly fresh but the cache absorbs little load — the cache hit rate is low because entries expire before being re-accessed, and the backend sees a steady stream of refreshes. A long TTL (1 hour–1 day) means cached data may be stale for up to the TTL, but the cache absorbs most of the load — hit rate is high and the backend is protected. The right value depends on the cost of staleness (a banking balance must be fresh; a product image can be hours old) and the cost of the backend call (a database query might be 50 ms; a third-party API call might be 500 ms and rate-limited). Operators typically pick a TTL that gives a hit rate of 90%+ while keeping staleness under the application's tolerance. Real-world: Stripe caches idempotency keys with a 24-hour TTL (long because the keys are immutable after creation); Netflix caches user watch progress with a 30-second TTL (short because users expect to see "continue watching" updates promptly); GitHub caches rendered README HTML with a 5-minute TTL (compromise between freshness after a push and the cost of re-rendering Markdown with syntax highlighting).

The **thundering herd problem** is TTL's headline failure mode, and it appears whenever many cached entries share the same expiration time. The classic scenario: a popular key is written to the cache with TTL = 60 seconds at T=0; over the next minute, thousands of clients read it from the cache (hits); at T=60 the entry expires; the next request misses, fetches from the backend, and re-populates the cache — but if the backend fetch takes 200 ms and the request rate is 10,000 QPS, 2,000 requests pile up before the cache is repopulated, all of them hitting the backend simultaneously. This is a **cache stampede** (covered in Topic 12), and the simplest mitigation is **TTL jitter**: instead of writing TTL = 60, write TTL = 60 + random(0, 10). The randomness spreads expirations across a 10-second window, so refreshes trickle rather than herd. Jitter is the cheapest, most universal stampede defense — it requires no coordination between clients and adds zero latency. Real-world: Cloudflare adds up to 10% jitter to all CDN TTLs to prevent synchronized re-fetches across POPs; Netflix's EVCache explicitly injects jitter into every TTL to avoid herd re-warming after deploys; AWS ElastiCache for Redis documents the pattern in its caching best-practices guide.

The **lazy vs active expiration** distinction affects CPU and memory. **Lazy expiration** (Redis's default for TTL) doesn't actively evict expired entries — instead, on every read, the cache checks the entry's deadline and evicts-on-read if expired. This means expired entries can sit in memory until they're accessed or until LRU/LFU evicts them, wasting memory but saving CPU on background sweeps. **Active expiration** (Redis's background sweep runs every 100 ms by default, sampling up to 20 expired keys per sweep) proactively evicts expired entries to reclaim memory. The combination is "active sweep for memory hygiene, lazy check on read for correctness." Memcached is purely lazy. Real-world: Redis's `hz` (frequency of background tasks) and `active-expire-effort` (1–10, aggressiveness of the sweep) are tunable; raising them helps if you have many short-TTL keys that you want to reclaim promptly, at the cost of CPU.

The **stale-while-revalidate (SWR)** pattern uses TTL as a soft signal rather than a hard cutoff. The entry has two TTLs: a fresh TTL (entry is definitely fresh) and a stale TTL (entry may be stale but is still served while a background refresh happens). On read: if within fresh TTL, serve immediately; if between fresh and stale TTL, serve the stale value AND trigger a background refresh; if past the stale TTL, miss and refresh synchronously. SWR gives the best of both worlds: the freshness of a short TTL with the load reduction of a long TTL, because the background refresh hides the backend latency from the user. HTTP's `Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=600` lets a CDN serve a stale response for up to 600 seconds while it refreshes in the background. Real-world: Cloudflare, Fastly, and Varnish all support SWR; React Query and SWR (the library) implement the same idea at the client; Caffeine and Caffeine-like caches support it server-side via `refreshAfterWrite`.

The **interaction with capacity-based eviction** is subtle. An entry with TTL = 1 hour but never accessed after the first read wastes memory for an hour; LRU/LFU would have evicted it earlier if the cache filled. The two policies compose: an entry is evicted either when its TTL expires OR when LRU/LFU picks it as a victim, whichever comes first. Most caches apply both: TTL provides a freshness bound, LRU/LFU provides a memory bound. Without LRU/LFU, a TTL-only cache with a long TTL and a high write rate will eventually evict everything via memory pressure (Memcached uses LRU; Redis uses LRU/LFU/noeviction). Without TTL, an LRU/LFU-only cache can serve stale data forever (until evicted), which is wrong for data that changes in the source — so TTL is the consistency mechanism and LRU/LFU is the capacity mechanism. Real-world: Redis deployments almost always combine `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru` (or lfu) with per-key EXPIRE; Memcached combines LRU with per-key expiration; CDNs combine Cache-Control max-age with capacity-based eviction at the POP.

The **per-key vs per-class TTL** decision affects operational complexity. Per-key TTL (every write specifies its own TTL) is flexible but requires the application to know the right TTL for every key, which is error-prone. Per-class TTL (the cache is partitioned by namespace, each namespace has a default TTL) is simpler: all user-profile keys get 5 minutes, all product-image keys get 1 day, all config keys get 60 seconds. Operators change one number per class rather than auditing every SET. Real-world: Netflix's EVCache configures per-app TTLs in a central property file; Discord configures per-namespace TTLs in their Redis proxy; Redis operators often use the key-prefix convention (`user:123`, `product:456`) to map prefixes to TTL policies enforced at the application layer.

### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Write[Write key K, TTL=60s] --> Store[Store: K=V, expires_at=now+60s]
    Store --> Read1[Read K at T=30s]
    Read1 --> Fresh1{expires_at > now?}
    Fresh1 -->|Yes| Hit1[Serve V from cache]
    Read2[Read K at T=61s] --> Fresh2{expires_at > now?}
    Fresh2 -->|No| Expired[Expired: miss or SWR]
    Expired --> Fetch[Fetch from DB]
    Fetch --> Repopulate[Re-store K=V, TTL=60+jitter]
    Repopulate --> Serve[Serve V]

    subgraph TTLTimeline[TTL Timeline]
        direction LR
        T0[T=0 write] --> T60[T=60 expires]
        T60 --> T61[T=61 miss]
        T61 --> T61p[T=61+ refresh + jitter]
    end
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
TTL = 60s on key K, written at T=0

Timeline (seconds):
  T=0   T=10  T=20  T=30  T=40  T=50  T=60  T=61  T=62
   |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |     |
   write ----------------------- hits ----- expire  refresh
   K=V,                              ^      v       ^
   expires_at=60s                    |      miss    re-store
                                    |              K=V,
                                    |              expires_at=122s
                              served until here    (with +1s jitter)

Without jitter (thundering herd):
  T=60: K expires
  T=60.001: 1000 concurrent reads all miss -> 1000x DB hits
  T=60.2:   cache repopulated, hits resume

With jitter (TTL = 60 + random(0, 10)):
  key K1:  expires at T=63
  key K2:  expires at T=67
  key K3:  expires at T=60
  key K4:  expires at T=69
  key K5:  expires at T=62
  + expirations spread across 10s window
  + refreshes trickle, no herd

  expirations (jittered):
   60 62 63 67 69   <-- spread out
    v  v  v  v  v
   DB DB DB DB DB   <-- 1x each, no spike

Lazy vs active expiration:
  + lazy:   check deadline on read, evict if expired
            (expired entries sit in memory until accessed)
  + active: background sweep evicts expired entries
            (reclaims memory proactively, costs CPU)
  + Redis:  both (active sweep hz=10/s, lazy check on read)
  + Memcached: lazy only

Stale-while-revalidate (SWR):
  T=0  T=30  T=60  T=90  T=600
   |    |     |     |     |
   write ---- fresh -- stale --- hard miss
                ^      ^
                |      |
                |      serve stale + background refresh
                serve fresh
```

### Walkthrough
1. **Write with TTL**: The application writes K=V to the cache with TTL=60s. The cache stores the value along with `expires_at = now + 60s`. Subsequent reads within the TTL window return the cached value.
2. **Read on hit (within TTL)**: At T=30, a read finds the entry and checks `expires_at` (T=60) against now (T=30); since 30 < 60, the entry is fresh and served from cache. The backend is not touched.
3. **Expiration**: At T=60, the entry's deadline passes. The next read at T=61 checks `expires_at` (60) against now (61); since 61 > 60, the entry is expired. The cache either returns a miss (synchronous refresh) or serves the stale value while triggering a background refresh (SWR). The refreshed entry is stored with TTL=60+jitter to avoid synchronized expirations.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- A TTL cache with optional jitter and stale-while-revalidate semantics.
- TTL cache with jitter to prevent thundering herd.
- Demonstrates: per-entry TTL, lazy expiration, jitter, stale-while-revalidate.
- Spread expirations across [ttl, ttl+jitter] to prevent synchronized
- Expiry (thundering herd) when many entries are written together.
- Expired: either SWR (serve stale, refresh in background)
- Or synchronous miss (caller waits for refresh).
- Fall through to synchronous refresh

```python
# TTL cache with jitter to prevent thundering herd.
# Demonstrates: per-entry TTL, lazy expiration, jitter, stale-while-revalidate.

import random
import threading
import time
from typing import Any, Optional, Callable

class TTLCache:
    """A TTL cache with optional jitter and stale-while-revalidate semantics.

    - On miss past TTL: refresh synchronously (default).
    - With swr=True:   serve stale value, refresh in background thread.
    - Jitter spreads expirations across [ttl, ttl+jitter] to avoid herds.
    """

    def __init__(self, ttl: float, jitter: float = 0.0, swr: bool = False):
        self.ttl = ttl
        self.jitter = jitter
        self.swr = swr
        self._store: dict = {}      # key -> (value, expires_at)
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        self._refreshing: set = set()
        self.stats = {"hits": 0, "misses": 0, "stale_served": 0, "refreshes": 0}

    def _make_expiry(self) -> float:
        # Spread expirations across [ttl, ttl+jitter] to prevent synchronized
        # expiry (thundering herd) when many entries are written together.
        return time.monotonic() + self.ttl + random.uniform(0, self.jitter)

    def get(self, key: Any, loader: Callable[[], Any]) -> Any:
        now = time.monotonic()
        with self._lock:
            entry = self._store.get(key)
            if entry is not None:
                value, expires_at = entry
                if now < expires_at:                       # fresh hit
                    self.stats["hits"] += 1
                    return value
                # Expired: either SWR (serve stale, refresh in background)
                # or synchronous miss (caller waits for refresh).
                if self.swr and key not in self._refreshing:
                    self.stats["stale_served"] += 1
                    self._refreshing.add(key)
                    threading.Thread(
                        target=self._refresh, args=(key, loader), daemon=True
                    ).start()
                    return value                            # stale but served
                # fall through to synchronous refresh
        # Synchronous refresh: only one caller hits the loader, others wait.
        return self._refresh_sync(key, loader)

    def _refresh_sync(self, key: Any, loader: Callable[[], Any]) -> Any:
        with self._lock:
            if key in self._refreshing:                    # another thread is refreshing
                self._lock.release()                       # wait briefly
                time.sleep(0.005)
                self._lock.acquire()
                entry = self._store.get(key)
                if entry and time.monotonic() < entry[1]:
                    return entry[0]
            self._refreshing.add(key)
        try:
            value = loader()
            with self._lock:
                self._store[key] = (value, self._make_expiry())
                self.stats["misses"] += 1
                self.stats["refreshes"] += 1
            return value
        finally:
            with self._lock:
                self._refreshing.discard(key)

    def _refresh(self, key: Any, loader: Callable[[], Any]) -> None:
        try:
            value = loader()
            with self._lock:
                self._store[key] = (value, self._make_expiry())
                self.stats["refreshes"] += 1
        finally:
            with self._lock:
                self._refreshing.discard(key)

    def set(self, key: Any, value: Any) -> None:
        with self._lock:
            self._store[key] = (value, self._make_expiry())

# ---- Demo: simulating a thundering herd with and without jitter ----
if __name__ == "__main__":
    call_count = {"db": 0}

    def expensive_db_read() -> str:
        call_count["db"] += 1
        time.sleep(0.05)                    # simulate 50ms DB query
        return f"payload-v{call_count['db']}"

    # Without jitter: 50 concurrent readers all hit the DB once.
    cache_no_jitter = TTLCache(ttl=0.1, jitter=0.0)
    threads = [
        threading.Thread(target=cache_no_jitter.get, args=("K", expensive_db_read))
        for _ in range(50)
    ]
    cache_no_jitter.set("K", "seed")        # warm with an entry that expires immediately
    time.sleep(0.11)                        # let it expire
    for t in threads: t.start()
    for t in threads: t.join()
    print(f"Without jitter: {call_count['db']} DB calls for 50 concurrent reads")

    # With jitter + SWR: DB called once, others get stale-then-fresh.
    call_count["db"] = 0
    cache_swj = TTLCache(ttl=0.1, jitter=0.05, swr=True)
    cache_swj.set("K", "seed")
    time.sleep(0.11)
    threads = [
        threading.Thread(target=cache_swj.get, args=("K", expensive_db_read))
        for _ in range(50)
    ]
    for t in threads: t.start()
    for t in threads: t.join()
    time.sleep(0.2)                         # let background refresh finish
    print(f"With jitter + SWR: {call_count['db']} DB calls for 50 concurrent reads")
    print(f"Stats: {cache_swj.stats}")
```

quiz.explanation: The TTL value controls the freshness-vs-load dial directly. A short TTL (e.g., 5 seconds) means cached data is at most 5 seconds old — very fresh — but the cache absorbs little load: every key that's accessed more than once per 5 seconds misses each window, and the backend sees a steady stream of refreshes (low hit rate).
